claim: Over 200 million confirmed cases of SARS-CoV2 have been reported since its emergence in China in late 2019.
source: Since the emergence of SARS-CoV2 in China in late 2019, over 200 million confirmed cases have been reported.
evidence: This is a factual statement about case numbers that represents established knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: Current vaccines designed to protect from original SARS-CoV-2 strains may have reduced potency for protection from infection against variants of concern.
source: The emergence of SARS-CoV2 variants of concern (VoCs) and evidence that existing vaccines that were designed to protect from the original strains of SARS-CoV-2 may have reduced potency for protection from infection against these VoC is driving continued development of second-generation vaccines that can protect against multiple VoC.
evidence: This statement references evidence from the scientific literature about vaccine efficacy against variants.

claim: Leading mRNA vaccines provide protection from severe COVID-19 disease and hospitalization in individuals infected with variants of concern.
source: While leading mRNA vaccines provide protection from severe COVID-19 disease and hospitalization in individuals infected with VoCs (Lopez Bernal et al., 2021), breakthrough infections, particularly in the upper airways of vaccinated individuals, are increasing and can lead to transmission events, even within clusters of vaccinated individuals (Brown et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lopez Bernal et al., 2021.

claim: Breakthrough infections in the upper airways of vaccinated individuals are increasing and can lead to transmission events, even within clusters of vaccinated individuals.
source: While leading mRNA vaccines provide protection from severe COVID-19 disease and hospitalization in individuals infected with VoCs (Lopez Bernal et al., 2021), breakthrough infections, particularly in the upper airways of vaccinated individuals, are increasing and can lead to transmission events, even within clusters of vaccinated individuals (Brown et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2021.

claim: Access to vaccines in less developed countries is still lacking.
source: In addition, although current vaccine candidates are widely available in developed countries, access to vaccines in less developed countries is still lacking (Fontanet et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fontanet et al., 2021.

claim: A VEEV-based replicating RNA vaccine encoding the spike protein of the original A.1 lineage of SARS-CoV2 delivered by LION was previously developed.
source: Previously, we reported the development of an Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV)-based replicating RNA (repRNA) vaccine encoding the spike protein of the original A.1 lineage of SARS-CoV2 delivered by a lipid inorganic nanoparticle (LION) (Erasmus et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Erasmus et al., 2020a).

claim: The repRNA/LION technology has been transitioned through current good manufacturing practices-compliant production.
source: We have since transitioned this technology through current good manufacturing practices-compliant production of both the repRNA and LION components and demonstrated safety and tolerability in a preclinical toxicology study leading to our open investigational new drug status under the drug product name, HDT-301, a B.1.351-specific vaccine that is pending phase I trials in US.
evidence: This is a statement about the development status of the technology.

claim: HDT-301, a B.1.351-specific vaccine, is pending phase I trials in the US.
source: We have since transitioned this technology through current good manufacturing practices-compliant production of both the repRNA and LION components and demonstrated safety and tolerability in a preclinical toxicology study leading to our open investigational new drug status under the drug product name, HDT-301, a B.1.351-specific vaccine that is pending phase I trials in US.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical development status of the vaccine.

claim: The repRNA/LION technology is currently being evaluated in a Phase I clinical trial in India under the drug product designation HGC019.
source: Additionally, this technology is currently being evaluated in a Phase I clinical trial in India under the drug product designation HGC019 with pending filings in Brazil, South Korea, and China.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical development status of the vaccine.

claim: Vaccination of mice or hamsters with LION/repRNA vaccines expressing spikes of distinct VoCs induced potent neutralizing antibody responses against each virus after a prime-boost regimen.
source: Vaccination of mice or hamsters with LION/repRNA vaccines expressing spikes of distinct VoCs induced potent neutralizing antibody (nAb) responses against each virus after a prime-boost regimen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vaccinated hamsters challenged with homologous SARS-CoV2 strains were completely protected from infection.
source: Vaccinated hamsters challenged with homologous SARS-CoV2 strains were completely protected from infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the hamster challenge studies.

claim: Vaccinated hamsters challenged with heterologous SARS-CoV-2 variants exhibited significantly reduced shedding of infectious virus.
source: In addition, vaccinated hamsters challenged with heterologous SARS-CoV-2 variants exhibited significantly reduced shedding of infectious virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the hamster challenge studies.

claim: Vaccinated hamsters challenged with heterologous viruses exhibited little-to-no viral-induced pathology in the lung tissue.
source: In addition, vaccinated hamsters challenged with heterologous viruses were significantly protected against viral shedding, viral replication, and exhibited little-to-no viral-induced pathology in the lung tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological data from the hamster challenge studies.

claim: The repRNA/LION vaccine can provide complete protection from exposure to homologous viruses.
source: Cumulatively, our data provide direct evidence that a repRNA/LION vaccine can provide complete protection from exposure to homologous viruses and substantial protection from disease via accelerated clearance of virus when exposed to a new heterologous VoC.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The repRNA/LION vaccine provides substantial protection from disease via accelerated clearance of virus when exposed to a new heterologous VoC.
source: Cumulatively, our data provide direct evidence that a repRNA/LION vaccine can provide complete protection from exposure to homologous viruses and substantial protection from disease via accelerated clearance of virus when exposed to a new heterologous VoC.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The relative potencies (EC50) of different repRNA constructs were not significantly different from each other, ranging from 15 to 21 ng of repRNA per well.
source: While differences in cell surface spike expression were observed at higher concentrations of LION/repRNA (Figure 1B), the relative potencies, in terms of half-maximal effective concentration (EC50), were not significantly different from each other, ranging from 15 to 21 ng of repRNA per well.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro potency assay data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The KV995PP mutation was associated with an increased signal at higher concentrations in the in vitro potency assay.
source: The differences at higher concentrations could either be due to variability in antibody binding or related to the mutations present in each spike, including the KV995PP mutation which was associated with an increased signal at the higher concentrations (optical densities of 0.6–2.1 for constructs 600 vs. 604, and 0.6–1.0 for constructs 675 vs. 676).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the in vitro potency assay data.

claim: Similar binding responses to the full-length S or to the S2 domain and RBD were observed between vaccine groups in mice.
source: In terms of the binding antibody characteristics, similar binding responses to the full-length S or to the S2 domain and RBD were observed between vaccine groups (Figure 2A), however the B.1.1.7- or B.1.351-vaccinated mice appeared to mount higher responses to the S1 domain with significantly higher S1-binding responses in the B.1.1.7-vaccinated mice compared to the ancestral A.1-vaccinated group.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: B.1.1.7-vaccinated mice had significantly higher S1-binding responses compared to the ancestral A.1-vaccinated group.
source: In terms of the binding antibody characteristics, similar binding responses to the full-length S or to the S2 domain and RBD were observed between vaccine groups (Figure 2A), however the B.1.1.7- or B.1.351-vaccinated mice appeared to mount higher responses to the S1 domain with significantly higher S1-binding responses in the B.1.1.7-vaccinated mice compared to the ancestral A.1-vaccinated group.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In native A.1 spike-vaccinated mice, there was a significant 4.4-fold drop in neutralization activity against B.1.1.7 challenge virus.
source: In terms of neutralization, in native A.1 spike-vaccinated mice, we observed similar neutralization activity against B.1 challenge virus compared to homologous A.1 challenge, while we found a significant 4.4-fold and 14.7-fold drop in neutralization activity against B.1.1.7 and B.1.351 challenge virus, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In native A.1 spike-vaccinated mice, there was a significant 14.7-fold drop in neutralization activity against B.1.351 challenge virus.
source: In terms of neutralization, in native A.1 spike-vaccinated mice, we observed similar neutralization activity against B.1 challenge virus compared to homologous A.1 challenge, while we found a significant 4.4-fold and 14.7-fold drop in neutralization activity against B.1.1.7 and B.1.351 challenge virus, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The pre-fusion-stabilized B.1 spike induced more breadth in specificity with only a 5.7-fold drop in neutralizing activity against B.1.351 virus.
source: In native- or pre-fusion B.1-spike-vaccinated mice, we observed similar magnitudes of neutralizing responses against A.1, B.1, and B.1.1.7 viruses between the two vaccines (Figure 2C and D), however the pre-fusion-stabilized B.1 spike appeared to induce more breadth in specificity with only a 5.7-fold drop in neutralizing activity against B.1.351 virus (Figure 2D), compared to a 29.3-fold drop in neutralizing activity against B.1.351 virus in mice that received the native conformation of the B.1 spike (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Native B.1 spike-vaccinated mice had a 29.3-fold drop in neutralizing activity against B.1.351 virus.
source: In native- or pre-fusion B.1-spike-vaccinated mice, we observed similar magnitudes of neutralizing responses against A.1, B.1, and B.1.1.7 viruses between the two vaccines (Figure 2C and D), however the pre-fusion-stabilized B.1 spike appeared to induce more breadth in specificity with only a 5.7-fold drop in neutralizing activity against B.1.351 virus (Figure 2D), compared to a 29.3-fold drop in neutralizing activity against B.1.351 virus in mice that received the native conformation of the B.1 spike (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In pre-fusion B.1.1.7-vaccinated mice, there was a significant 11.3-fold drop in neutralization activity against the B.1.351 VoC compared to homologous B.1.1.7 virus.
source: In pre-fusion B.1.1.7-vaccinated mice, we found a significant 11.3-fold drop in neutralization activity against the B.1.351 VoC compared to homologous B.1.1.7 virus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In B.1.351-vaccinated mice, there was a significant 12.3-fold drop in neutralization activity against the B.1.1.7 challenge virus.
source: In B.1.351-vaccinated mice, we found a significant 12.3-fold and 4-fold drop in neutralization activity against the B.1.1.7 and A.1 challenge virus, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In B.1.351-vaccinated mice, there was a 4-fold drop in neutralization activity against the A.1 challenge virus.
source: In B.1.351-vaccinated mice, we found a significant 12.3-fold and 4-fold drop in neutralization activity against the B.1.1.7 and A.1 challenge virus, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The B.1.351 VoC was the most resistant to neutralizing antibodies elicited by A.1, B.1, or B.1.1.7 vaccination.
source: Cumulatively, our data show that the B.1.351 VoC was the most resistant to nAbs elicited by A.1, B.1, or B.1.1.7 vaccination.
evidence: This claim is based on the neutralization data from the mouse studies.

claim: Each vaccine candidate elicited robust neutralizing antibody titers ranging from 1:320 to 1:10,240 against homologous virus in hamsters.
source: Against homologous virus, each vaccine candidate elicited robust nAb titers ranging from 1:320 to 1:10,240 with 2- to 14-fold reductions when measured against heterologous virus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neutralizing antibody titers showed 2- to 14-fold reductions when measured against heterologous virus in hamsters.
source: Against homologous virus, each vaccine candidate elicited robust nAb titers ranging from 1:320 to 1:10,240 with 2- to 14-fold reductions when measured against heterologous virus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The B.1.351 strain was the most 'vaccine-resistant' VoC, with 13- to 14-fold reductions in nAb titers in hamsters immunized with A.1- or B.1.1.7-specific vaccines.
source: As observed in mice, the most 'vaccine-resistant' VoC was the B.1.351 strain, where 13- to 14-fold reductions in nAb titers were observed in hamsters immunized with A.1- or B.1.1.7-specific vaccines, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The A.1 and B.1.1.7 strains of SARS-CoV2 were similarly neutralized by A.1 or B.1.1.7 vaccination exhibiting a roughly 2-fold reduction in neutralizing activity when comparing homologous to heterologous challenge.
source: The A.1 and B.1.1.7 strains of SARS-CoV2 were similarly neutralized by A.1 or B.1.1.7 vaccination exhibiting a roughly 2-fold reduction in neutralizing activity when comparing homologous to heterologous challenge, however, an ~4- to 5-fold reduction in nAb titer was observed against these viruses in hamsters receiving the B.1.351-specific vaccine (Figure 3), recapitulating observations in mice (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An approximately 4- to 5-fold reduction in nAb titer was observed against A.1 and B.1.1.7 viruses in hamsters receiving the B.1.351-specific vaccine.
source: The A.1 and B.1.1.7 strains of SARS-CoV2 were similarly neutralized by A.1 or B.1.1.7 vaccination exhibiting a roughly 2-fold reduction in neutralizing activity when comparing homologous to heterologous challenge, however, an ~4- to 5-fold reduction in nAb titer was observed against these viruses in hamsters receiving the B.1.351-specific vaccine (Figure 3), recapitulating observations in mice (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Against the B.1.617.2 VoC, the A.1 and B.1.1.7 spike-vaccinated hamsters had a 4- to 6-fold reduction in serum neutralization titer compared to homologous virus challenge.
source: Against the B.1.617.2 VoC, the A.1 and B.1.1.7 spike-vaccinated hamsters had a 4- to 6-fold reduction in serum neutralization titer compared to homologous virus challenge while hamsters vaccinated with the B.1.351 spike had a 10-fold reduction in neutralization titer (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Hamsters vaccinated with the B.1.351 spike had a 10-fold reduction in neutralization titer against the B.1.617.2 VoC.
source: Against the B.1.617.2 VoC, the A.1 and B.1.1.7 spike-vaccinated hamsters had a 4- to 6-fold reduction in serum neutralization titer compared to homologous virus challenge while hamsters vaccinated with the B.1.351 spike had a 10-fold reduction in neutralization titer (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PRNT80 data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The median infectious dose (ID50) in hamsters for the A.1 strain is 5 TCID50.
source: For reference, the median infectious dose (ID50) in hamsters for the A.1 strain is 5 TCID50 (Rosenke et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosenke et al., 2020.

claim: Against the A.1 strain, only vaccination with the B.1.1.7 repRNA significantly reduced Sg RNA levels in oral swabs.
source: Against the A.1 strain, only vaccination with the B.1.1.7 repRNA significantly reduced Sg RNA levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All three repRNAs significantly reduced shedding of infectious virus in the oral cavity at day 2 PI against A.1 challenge.
source: However, all three repRNAs significantly reduced shedding of infectious virus in the oral cavity at day 2 PI and both the A.1 and B.1.1.7 repRNAs significantly reduced infectious virus at day 4 PI (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both the A.1 and B.1.1.7 repRNAs significantly reduced infectious virus at day 4 PI against A.1 challenge.
source: However, all three repRNAs significantly reduced shedding of infectious virus in the oral cavity at day 2 PI and both the A.1 and B.1.1.7 repRNAs significantly reduced infectious virus at day 4 PI (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No infectious virus could be isolated from the swabs of B.1.17 repRNA-vaccinated animals at day 4 PI following A.1 challenge.
source: Notably, no infectious virus could be isolated from the swabs of B.1.17 repRNA-vaccinated animals at day 4 PI (Table 1), indicating rapid control of viral shedding.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Against the SARS-CoV2 A.1 strain, vaccination with any of the three repRNAs can significantly reduce viral shedding.
source: These data indicate that against the SARS-CoV2 A.1 strain, vaccination with any of the three repRNAs can significantly reduce viral shedding.
evidence: This claim is based on the viral shedding data from A.1 challenge experiments.

claim: Against the B.1.351 variant, hamsters vaccinated with the homologous B.1.351 repRNA had significantly reduced Sg RNA at day 2 PI.
source: Against the B.1.351 variant, compared to mock-vaccinated hamsters at day 2 PI, hamsters vaccinated with the homologous B.1.351 repRNA had significantly reduced Sg RNA (Figure 4C) and by day 4 PI, significantly reduced viral RNA was seen in all vaccinated hamsters (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: By day 4 PI, significantly reduced viral RNA was seen in all vaccinated hamsters challenged with B.1.351.
source: Against the B.1.351 variant, compared to mock-vaccinated hamsters at day 2 PI, hamsters vaccinated with the homologous B.1.351 repRNA had significantly reduced Sg RNA (Figure 4C) and by day 4 PI, significantly reduced viral RNA was seen in all vaccinated hamsters (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Against the B.1.351 variant challenge, vaccination with any of the repRNAs significantly reduced infectious virus at both day 2 and 4 PI.
source: Similar to the A.1 challenge, against the B.1.351 variant challenge, vaccination with any of the repRNAs significantly reduced infectious virus at both day 2 and 4 PI (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At day 2 PI, infectious virus could only be isolated from the oral cavity of 2 of 6 hamsters vaccinated with the B.1.351 repRNA following B.1.351 challenge.
source: Notably, at day 2 PI, infectious virus could only be isolated from the oral cavity of 2 of 6 hamsters vaccinated with the B.1.351 repRNA, while virus was isolated from 6 of 6 vaccinated with the A.1 or 3 of 6 vaccinated with the B.1.1.7 vaccine (Table 1), suggesting more rapid clearance of virus in B.1.351-infected hamsters vaccinated with B.1.351 repRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Against the B.1.1.7 variant, the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 vaccine repRNAs significantly reduced Sg RNA at day 2 PI.
source: Finally, against the B.1.1.7 variant, the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 vaccine repRNAs significantly reduced Sg RNA at day 2 PI, and at day 4 PI both the A.1 and B.1.351 repRNAs significantly reduced Sg RNA (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At day 4 PI, both the A.1 and B.1.351 repRNAs significantly reduced Sg RNA against B.1.1.7 challenge.
source: Finally, against the B.1.1.7 variant, the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 vaccine repRNAs significantly reduced Sg RNA at day 2 PI, and at day 4 PI both the A.1 and B.1.351 repRNAs significantly reduced Sg RNA (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Against B.1.1.7 challenge, vaccination with any of the repRNAs led to significantly reduced titers of infectious virus in oral swabs at both day 2 and 4 PI.
source: Similar to A.1 or B.1.351 variant challenges, vaccination with any of the repRNAs lead to significantly reduced titers of infectious virus in oral swabs at both day 2 and 4 PI (Figure 4F), and more rapid clearance of virus was observed in vaccine-matched B.1.1.7-vaccinated/challenged animals, with live virus isolated in oral cavities only 1 of 6 B.1.1.7-vaccinated hamsters.
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Live virus was isolated in oral cavities of only 1 of 6 B.1.1.7-vaccinated hamsters at day 2 PI following B.1.1.7 challenge.
source: Similar to A.1 or B.1.351 variant challenges, vaccination with any of the repRNAs lead to significantly reduced titers of infectious virus in oral swabs at both day 2 and 4 PI (Figure 4F), and more rapid clearance of virus was observed in vaccine-matched B.1.1.7-vaccinated/challenged animals, with live virus isolated in oral cavities only 1 of 6 B.1.1.7-vaccinated hamsters.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 4F.

claim: Across all three SARS-CoV2 challenges, 19 of 54 vaccinated hamsters had no detectable infectious virus in their swabs at day 2 PI.
source: Overall, across all three SARS-CoV2 challenges, 19 of 54 and 32 of 54 vaccinated hamsters had no detectable infectious virus in their swabs at day 2 and 4 PI, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Across all three SARS-CoV2 challenges, 32 of 54 vaccinated hamsters had no detectable infectious virus in their swabs at day 4 PI.
source: Overall, across all three SARS-CoV2 challenges, 19 of 54 and 32 of 54 vaccinated hamsters had no detectable infectious virus in their swabs at day 2 and 4 PI, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Vaccination with any of the three repRNAs significantly reduced viral shedding against homologous and heterologous SARS-CoV2 challenge with more rapid clearance observed in vaccine-matched VoC challenges.
source: Cumulatively, these data demonstrate that vaccination with any of the three repRNAs significantly reduced viral shedding against homologous and heterologous SARS-CoV2 challenge with more rapid clearance observed in vaccine-matched VoC challenges.
evidence: This claim is based on the viral shedding data from all challenge experiments.

claim: All three vaccine repRNAs significantly reduced Sg viral RNA in the lungs of hamsters challenged with any of the three variants of SARS-CoV2.
source: All three vaccine repRNAs significantly reduced Sg viral RNA in the lungs of hamsters challenged with any of the three variants of SARS-CoV2 (Figure 5A, C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A, C, and E.

claim: The majority of vaccinated animals across the three SARS-CoV2 variant challenges had no detectable Sg RNA in the lungs.
source: Notably, the majority of vaccinated animals across the three SARS-CoV2 variant challenges had no detectable Sg RNA, suggestive of substantial immunity in the lungs of these animals.
evidence: This claim is based on the qRT-PCR data from lung tissue.

claim: All three RNA vaccines significantly reduced infectious virus in the lungs of animals challenged with any of the three SARS-CoV2 variants.
source: We also quantified the amount of infectious virus in the lungs and found that all three RNA vaccines significantly reduced infectious virus in animals challenged with any of the three SARS-CoV2 variants (Figure 5B, D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 data shown in Figure 5B, D, and F.

claim: Against infection with the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 variants, no infectious virus was detected in the lungs of any vaccinated hamster.
source: Against infection with the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 variants, no infectious virus was detected in the lungs of any vaccinated hamster (Figure 5B, D and F and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 data shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Against the A.1 strain, infectious virus was only found in the lungs of 1 of 6 animals in the A.1 and B.1.351 repRNA-vaccinated animals and 0 of 6 animals in the B.1.1.7 repRNA-vaccinated animals.
source: Against the A.1 strain, infectious virus was only found in the lungs of 1 of 6 animals in the A.1 and B.1.351 repRNA-vaccinated animals and 0 of 6 animals in the B.1.1.7 repRNA-vaccinated animals (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Vaccination with any of the repRNAs resulted in significant reduction of SARS-CoV2 burden in the lungs.
source: Cumulatively, by highly sensitive qRT-PCR for Sg RNA and by measurement of infectious virus, vaccination with any of the repRNAs resulted in significant reduction of SARS-CoV2 burden in the lungs indicating that the LION/repRNA vaccine platform is highly protective against SARS-CoV2 infection in the lung.
evidence: This claim is based on the lung viral burden data.

claim: The LION/repRNA vaccine platform is highly protective against SARS-CoV2 infection in the lung.
source: Cumulatively, by highly sensitive qRT-PCR for Sg RNA and by measurement of infectious virus, vaccination with any of the repRNAs resulted in significant reduction of SARS-CoV2 burden in the lungs indicating that the LION/repRNA vaccine platform is highly protective against SARS-CoV2 infection in the lung.
evidence: This claim is based on the lung viral burden data.

claim: Mock-vaccinated hamsters challenged with A.1 or B.1.1.7 strains of SARS-CoV2 developed lesions typical of SARS-CoV2.
source: H&E staining of lung sections demonstrated that among mock-vaccinated hamsters challenged with A.1 or B.1.1.7 strains of SARS-CoV2 developed lesions typical of SARS-CoV2 with the A.1 and B.1.1.7 variant-infected hamsters developing more, and more severe, lesions than those infected with the B.1.351 variant.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A.1 and B.1.1.7 variant-infected hamsters developed more, and more severe, lesions than those infected with the B.1.351 variant.
source: H&E staining of lung sections demonstrated that among mock-vaccinated hamsters challenged with A.1 or B.1.1.7 strains of SARS-CoV2 developed lesions typical of SARS-CoV2 with the A.1 and B.1.1.7 variant-infected hamsters developing more, and more severe, lesions than those infected with the B.1.351 variant.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hamsters vaccinated with any of the repRNAs were protected from lung pathology and had diminished viral antigen.
source: In contrast, hamsters vaccinated with any of the repRNAs were protected from lung pathology and had diminished viral antigen (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological and IHC data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The majority of vaccinated hamsters had no evident lesions and no detectable viral antigen.
source: The majority of hamsters had no evident lesions and no detectable viral antigen and in the few that had lesions or IHC reactivity, they were minor (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological and IHC data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hamsters vaccinated with any of the three repRNAs and challenged with either the A.1 or B.1.1.7 variant had significantly reduced lung-to-body weight ratios compared to similarly challenged mock-vaccinated hamsters.
source: Hamsters vaccinated with any of the three repRNAs and challenged with either the A.1 or B.1.1.7 variant had significantly reduced lung-to-body weight ratios compared to similarly challenged mock-vaccinated hamsters (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lung weight data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: Against the B.1.351 variant, only hamsters vaccinated with the A.1 repRNA had significantly reduced lung-to-body weight ratio compared to mock-vaccinated hamsters.
source: Against the B.1.351 variant, only hamsters vaccinated with the A.1 repRNA had significantly reduced lung-to-body weight ratio compared to mock-vaccinated hamsters (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lung weight data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: All vaccines conferred significant protection against lung pathology and significantly reduced viral antigen induced by any of the SARS-CoV2 challenge strains.
source: Cumulative pathology scores of H&E stained (Figure 7D-F) or lung sections stained for viral antigen (Figure 7G-I) showed that all vaccines conferred significant protection against lung pathology and significantly reduced viral antigen induced by any of the SARS-CoV2 challenge strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathology scoring data shown in Figure 7D-I.

claim: Mock-vaccinated B.1.351 challenged hamsters had reduced viral loads and reduced evidence of virally induced pathology than mock-vaccinated hamsters challenged with either the A.1 or B.1.1.7 VoC.
source: Overall mock-vaccinated B.1.351 challenged hamsters had reduced viral loads (Figure 5) and reduced evidence of virally induced pathology (Figure 7B, E and H) than mock-vaccinated hamsters challenged with either the A.1 or B.1.1.7 VoC suggesting B.1.351 infection was milder in these hamsters.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of viral load and pathology data across challenge groups.

claim: B.1.351 infection was milder in hamsters than A.1 or B.1.1.7 infection.
source: Overall mock-vaccinated B.1.351 challenged hamsters had reduced viral loads (Figure 5) and reduced evidence of virally induced pathology (Figure 7B, E and H) than mock-vaccinated hamsters challenged with either the A.1 or B.1.1.7 VoC suggesting B.1.351 infection was milder in these hamsters.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the viral load and pathology data.

claim: As of early 2022, the COVID-19 pandemic continues with resurgent case numbers in multiple countries despite widespread vaccine deployment.
source: Despite the availability of several vaccines for SARS-CoV2 in the majority of the developed world, as of early 2022, the COVID-19 pandemic continues with resurgent case numbers in multiple countries despite widespread vaccine deployment (WHO, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO, 2021.

claim: Existing vaccines have diminished efficacy against Delta and Omicron VoCs compared to previous VoC.
source: The emergence of the Delta VoC, more recently Omicron (B.1.1.529), and emerging evidence that existing vaccines have diminished efficacy against these VoCs compared to previous VoC (Ai et al., 2022; Carreño et al., 2022; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021; Sheikh et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2021) together indicate that continued development of vaccines for COVID-19 is warranted.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Ai et al., 2022; Carreño et al., 2022; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021; Sheikh et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2021).

claim: Continued development of vaccines for COVID-19 is warranted.
source: The emergence of the Delta VoC, more recently Omicron (B.1.1.529), and emerging evidence that existing vaccines have diminished efficacy against these VoCs compared to previous VoC (Ai et al., 2022; Carreño et al., 2022; Lopez Bernal et al., 2021; Sheikh et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2021) together indicate that continued development of vaccines for COVID-19 is warranted.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the evidence about diminished vaccine efficacy against new variants.

claim: Mice vaccinated with a lipid nanoparticle delivered VEEV repRNA expressing the pre-fusion-stabilized form of the original Wuhan SARS-CoV2 isolate developed potent nAb responses against infectious SARS-CoV2.
source: In mice vaccinated with a lipid nanoparticle delivered VEEV repRNA expressing the pre-fusion-stabilized form of the original Wuhan SARS-CoV2 isolate, mice developed potent nAb responses against infectious SARS-CoV2 (McKay et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKay et al., 2020.

claim: A DNA-launched Semliki-forest virus replicon expressing the Wuhan SARS-CoV2 isolate spike-induced humoral and cellular immunity against SARS-CoV2 in mice.
source: Similarly, a DNA-launched Semliki-forest virus replicon expressing the Wuhan SARS-CoV2 isolate spike-induced humoral and cellular immunity against SARS-CoV2 in mice (Szurgot et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szurgot et al., 2021.

claim: The LION/repRNA vaccine expressing the native A.1 spike induced potent nAb activity in mice and pigtail macaques.
source: We have previously evaluated the LION/repRNA vaccine expressing the native A.1 spike in mice and pigtail macaques and found that vaccination-induced potent nAb activity (Erasmus et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Erasmus et al., 2020a).

claim: Vaccinated pigtail macaques were protected against SARS-CoV2 challenge.
source: Challenge studies showed vaccinated pigtail macaques were protected against SARS-CoV2 challenge (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This claim references unpublished data (manuscript in preparation).

claim: Reduced neutralization of convalescent and A.1-vaccinated sera against the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 variants has been previously shown.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing reduced neutralization of convalescent and A.1-vaccinated sera against the B.1.351 and B.1.1.7 variants (Shen et al., 2021a; Shen et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021) and provides new insights into the design of VoC-specific vaccines and their ability to provide cross-neutralizing immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Shen et al., 2021a; Shen et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).

claim: The B.1.617.2 (Delta) VoC exhibited a 6-fold reduction in nAb titers in A.1-vaccinated hamsters.
source: Similar to recent reports (Edara et al., 2021; Planas et al., 2021), the B.1.617.2 VoC exhibited a 6-fold reduction in nAb titers in A.1-vaccinated hamsters, and B.1.351 VoC still remained the most resistant to A.1 vaccination.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to Edara et al., 2021 and Planas et al., 2021.

claim: B.1.1.7 vaccination induced robust cross-neutralization of B.1.617.2 with only a 3.5-fold reduction in nAb titers relative to homologous neutralization.
source: Interestingly, B.1.1.7 vaccination induced robust cross-neutralization of B.1.617.2 with only a 3.5-fold reduction in nAb titers relative to homologous neutralization.
evidence: This claim is based on neutralization data from the hamster study.

claim: Vaccination with B.1.351 did not provide very robust cross-neutralization of B.1.617.2, with a 10-fold reduction in nAb titers relative to homologous neutralization.
source: Vaccination with B.1.351, however, did not provide very robust cross-neutralization of B.1.617.2, with a 10-fold reduction in nAb titers relative to homologous neutralization, suggesting that those previously infected with B.1.351 may remain susceptible to re-infection with the B.1.617.2 VoC.
evidence: This claim is based on neutralization data from the hamster study.

claim: Those previously infected with B.1.351 may remain susceptible to re-infection with the B.1.617.2 VoC.
source: Vaccination with B.1.351, however, did not provide very robust cross-neutralization of B.1.617.2, with a 10-fold reduction in nAb titers relative to homologous neutralization, suggesting that those previously infected with B.1.351 may remain susceptible to re-infection with the B.1.617.2 VoC.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the neutralization data.

claim: Despite sterilizing protection in the lower airway of vaccinated hamsters challenged with homologous virus, transmission was still observed upon co-housing with naïve animals.
source: Indeed, a recent study demonstrated that despite sterilizing protection in the lower airway of vaccinated hamsters challenged with homologous virus, transmission was still observed upon co-housing with naïve animals (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: In ChAdOx1 nCoV-19-vaccinated hamsters, vaccination reduced shedding of SARS-CoV2 in B.1.1.7 challenged but not B.1.351 challenged hamsters, despite sterile protection in the lungs.
source: In ChAdOx1 nCoV-19-vaccinated hamsters, vaccination reduced shedding of SARS-CoV2 in B.1.1.7 challenged but not B.1.351 challenged hamsters, despite sterile protection in the lungs (Fischer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2021.

claim: In ChAdOx1 nCov-19-vaccinated rhesus macaques, no differences in SARS-CoV2 RNA loads in nasal swabs between vaccinated or unvaccinated animals were observed despite significantly reduced viral loads in the lungs.
source: In ChAdOx1 nCov-19-vaccinated rhesus macaques, no differences in SARS-CoV2 RNA loads in nasal swabs between vaccinated or unvaccinated animals were observed despite significantly reduced viral loads in the lungs (van Doremalen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van Doremalen et al., 2020.

claim: Intranasal but not IM vaccination with ChAd nCoV-19 resulted in significantly reduced viral shedding.
source: Intranasal delivery of the ChAd nCoV-19 vaccine may improve control of viral shedding as intranasal but not IM vaccination resulted in significantly reduced viral shedding (Hassan et al., 2021; van Doremalen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hassan et al., 2021 and van Doremalen et al., 2021.

claim: Rhesus macaques vaccinated with mRNA-1273 showed significantly reduced viral RNA in both bronchoalveolar-lavage (BAL) and nasal swabs.
source: In contrast, rhesus macaques vaccinated with mRNA-1273 showed significantly reduced viral RNA in both bronchoalveolar-lavage (BAL) and nasal swabs (Corbett et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Corbett et al., 2020.

claim: Rhesus macaques vaccinated with Ad26 had significantly reduced upper and lower respiratory titers although more robust protection was observed in the BAL than nasal swabs.
source: Similarly, rhesus macaques vaccinated with Ad26 had significantly reduced upper and lower respiratory titers although across vaccine candidates evaluated, more robust protection was observed in the BAL than nasal swabs (Mercado et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mercado et al., 2020.

claim: An inactivated rabies virus-vectored approach was able to induce sterilizing protection in the upper airway of a majority of hamsters.
source: An important consideration of the above referenced studies is that these were within the context of A.1 vaccination and matched A.1 viral challenge; therefore, continued evaluation of deployed vaccines and those under development against emergent VoCs is needed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kurup et al., 2021.

claim: The A.1-specific repRNA could induce T-cell responses in mice and non-human primates.
source: However, we have previously shown that our A.1-specific repRNA could induce T-cell responses in mice and non-human primates (Erasmus et al., 2020a) indicating this vaccine can induce T-cell responses in vaccinated animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Erasmus et al., 2020a).

claim: Neutralizing antibodies have been shown to strongly correlate with vaccine-mediated protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Furthermore, nAbs have been shown to strongly correlate with vaccine-mediated protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection (Khoury et al., 2021) and our data showed that vaccination with our A.1- or B.1.1.7-specific repRNA could induce heterologous neutralizing activity even against the B.1.617.2 VoC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khoury et al., 2021.

claim: Vaccination with A.1- or B.1.1.7-specific repRNA could induce heterologous neutralizing activity even against the B.1.617.2 VoC.
source: Furthermore, nAbs have been shown to strongly correlate with vaccine-mediated protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection (Khoury et al., 2021) and our data showed that vaccination with our A.1- or B.1.1.7-specific repRNA could induce heterologous neutralizing activity even against the B.1.617.2 VoC.
evidence: This claim is based on neutralization data from the study.

claim: LION/repRNA vaccines can induce broadly protective immunity against multiple SARS-CoV2 strains.
source: Together our data demonstrate that LION/repRNA vaccines can induce broadly protective immunity against multiple SARS-CoV2 strains.
evidence: This claim is based on the cumulative data from the study.

claim: Vaccination significantly reduced SARS-CoV2 viral burden in both the upper and lower respiratory tract.
source: Vaccination significantly reduced SARS-CoV2 viral burden in both the upper and lower respiratory tract and prevented development of SARS-CoV2 lung pathology even when challenged with heterologous SARS-CoV2 strains.
evidence: This claim is based on the viral burden and pathology data from the study.

claim: Vaccination prevented development of SARS-CoV2 lung pathology even when challenged with heterologous SARS-CoV2 strains.
source: Vaccination significantly reduced SARS-CoV2 viral burden in both the upper and lower respiratory tract and prevented development of SARS-CoV2 lung pathology even when challenged with heterologous SARS-CoV2 strains.
evidence: This claim is based on the pathology data from the study.

claim: A bivalent mixture consisting of B.1.1.7- and B.1.351-specific vaccines may provide superior cross-neutralizing capacity than each monovalent vaccine alone.
source: Additionally, given the distinct heterologous nAb responses elicited by B.1.1.7- or B.1.351-specific repRNA, coupled with the observation that matched vaccination provides superior protection in the upper airway against homologous VoC challenge, a bivalent mixture consisting of these two VoC-specific vaccines may provide superior cross-neutralizing capacity than each monovalent vaccine alone.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data.

claim: Matched vaccination provides superior protection in the upper airway against homologous VoC challenge.
source: Additionally, given the distinct heterologous nAb responses elicited by B.1.1.7- or B.1.351-specific repRNA, coupled with the observation that matched vaccination provides superior protection in the upper airway against homologous VoC challenge, a bivalent mixture consisting of these two VoC-specific vaccines may provide superior cross-neutralizing capacity than each monovalent vaccine alone.
evidence: This claim is based on the viral shedding data from the study.

claim: A vaccine approach in which the vaccine is matched to a VoC may provide optimal immunity which may decrease the frequency of vaccine breakthrough-mediated transmission events.
source: Our data also support a vaccine approach in which the vaccine is matched to a VoC to provide optimal immunity which may decrease the frequency of vaccine breakthrough-mediated transmission events, an important consideration for the rapid emergence of the B.1.529 (Omicron) VoC (Ai et al., 2022; Carreño et al., 2022; Kuhlmann et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data and supported by citations.

claim: The vaccine platform is amenable to rapid updates to specifically target emergent VoCs.
source: Furthermore, our vaccine platform is amenable to rapid updates to specifically target emergent VoCs and our data cumulatively support continued development of the LION/repRNA vaccine platform for COVID-19.
evidence: This claim is based on the demonstrated ability to create variant-specific vaccines.
